claim: EGR1 is a locus that strongly responds to the activation of a majority of the recognized protein kinase oncogenes, including 30 receptor tyrosine kinases and 154 of their disease-associated mutants.
source: We used FGF-receptor signaling to identify EGR1 as a locus that strongly responds to the activation of a majority of the recognized protein kinase oncogenes, including 30 receptor tyrosine kinases and 154 of their disease-associated mutants.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that 30 wild-type RTKs (81%) and 154 (71%) of their mutants induced EGR1 when expressed in 293T cells, as demonstrated in Figures 2-4.

claim: The EGR1 promoter was engineered to enhance trans-activation capacity and optimized for simple screening assays with luciferase or fluorescent reporters.
source: The EGR1 promoter was engineered to enhance trans-activation capacity and optimized for simple screening assays with luciferase or fluorescent reporters.
evidence: The manuscript describes four successive rounds of optimization that identified a 402nt-long region critical for FGF2-mediated trans-activation, and the development of pKrox24 reporters with luciferase and fluorescent variants.

claim: Nilotinib targets LTK and INSR as novel targets not previously reported.
source: Figure 5A shows that all tested TKIs inhibited RTKs that had already been reported as targets in literature (Supplementary file 1E), with exception of LTK and INSR, which were identified as two novel targets for nilotinib (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E demonstrating nilotinib inhibition of LTK and INSR, which were not previously reported as targets according to Supplementary file 1E.

claim: Osimertinib inhibits LTK in both wild-type and mutant forms.
source: However, LTK was an exception, as it appeared to be inhibited by osimertinib in both wt and mutant forms.
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figure 5B-C showing osimertinib-mediated inhibition of LTK activity in wild-type and mutant forms through pKrox24 reporter assays and immunoblot analyses.

claim: A majority of known RTKs activate the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK MAP kinase signaling module.
source: A majority of known RTKs activate the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK MAP kinase signaling module, a pathway that links extracellular mitogenic signals to gene transcription (Vogelstein et al., 2013; Meloche and Pouysségur, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Vogelstein et al., 2013; Meloche and Pouysségur, 2007).

claim: FGF2 treatment induced Egr1, Egr2, Nr4A2, Dusp6 and Rgs1 among the most strongly induced genes in multiple myeloma and rat chondrosarcoma cells.
source: The expression profiling of cells treated with FGFR ligand FGF2 identified Egr1, Egr2, Nr4A2, Dusp6 and Rgs1 among the most strongly induced genes (Krejci et al., 2010; Buchtova et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Krejci et al., 2010; Buchtova et al., 2015) that performed expression profiling.

claim: EGR1 promoter showed the strongest response to FGF2 treatment, being trans-activated approximately 12-fold in RCS cells.
source: In dual-luciferase activity assays performed in RCS cells, EGR1 promoter showed the strongest response, as it was trans-activated approximately 12-fold following FGF2 treatment (Figure 1A), and was therefore chosen for subsequent studies.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from dual-luciferase assays shown in Figure 1A demonstrating 12-fold trans-activation of the EGR1 promoter.

claim: FGF2 induced endogenous EGR1 protein expression in seven different cell types tested.
source: FGF2 induced endogenous EGR1 protein expression in seven different cell types tested, and this phenotype was dependent on ERK activation (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing EGR1 induction across multiple cell types.

claim: FGF2-mediated EGR1 induction is dependent on ERK activation.
source: FGF2 induced endogenous EGR1 protein expression in seven different cell types tested, and this phenotype was dependent on ERK activation (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing that ERK MAP kinase pathway inhibitor PD0325901 blocks FGF2-mediated EGR1 induction.

claim: A 402nt-long region (−799/–397 relative to TSS) is critical for FGF2-mediated trans-activation of the EGR1 promoter.
source: Four successive rounds of 3- and/or 5-prime sequence shortening and optimization identified a 402nt-long region (−799/–397 relative to TSS) that is critical for FGF2-mediated trans-activation (called D-E element) of the EGR1 promoter (Figure 1B–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from four rounds of promoter optimization shown in Figures 1B-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Addition of two extra copies of the D-E element into the EGR1 promoter enhanced its response to FGF2 by approximately 50%.
source: The addition of two extra copies of the D-E element into the EGR1 promoter (hEGR1-D) enhanced its response to FGF2 by approximately 50% (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1E showing enhanced trans-activation with additional D-E elements.

claim: pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc FGF2-mediated trans-activation in RCS cells peaked at approximately 40 ng/ml FGF2.
source: The level of pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc FGF2-mediated trans-activation in RCS cells peaked at approximately 40 ng/ml FGF2.
evidence: The manuscript presents dose-response data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 showing peak trans-activation at 40 ng/ml FGF2.

claim: Treatment of RCS cells with higher doses of FGF2 further elevated ERK activation but had a negligible effect on pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc activity.
source: Treatment of RCS cells with higher doses of FGF2 further elevated ERK activation (Krejci et al., 2007), but had a negligible effect on pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), implying that it is unlikely that further development of the pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc promoter sequence would yield a significant increase in trans-activation capacity.
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and cites previous work (Krejci et al., 2007) showing ERK activation increases but reporter activity plateaus.

claim: pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc responded to the activation of FGFR signaling following FGF2 addition in five different cell types tested.
source: In the five different cell types tested, pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc responded to the activation of FGFR signaling following FGF2 addition, as well as to the chemical inhibition of endogenous FGFR signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 showing reporter response across multiple cell types.

claim: pKrox24(MapErk)Luc showed no additional increase in FGF2-mediated trans-activation compared to pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc.
source: When compared to pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc, pKrox24(MapErk)Luc showed no additional increase in FGF2-mediated trans-activation, but possessed a significantly lower basal activity in RCS and 293T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 showing similar trans-activation levels between the two reporters.

claim: pKrox24(MapErk)Luc possessed a significantly lower basal activity in RCS and 293T cells compared to pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc.
source: When compared to pKrox24(2xD-E_inD)Luc, pKrox24(MapErk)Luc showed no additional increase in FGF2-mediated trans-activation, but possessed a significantly lower basal activity in RCS and 293T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7B showing lower basal activity of pKrox24(MapErk)Luc.

claim: Fluorescent reporters with dTomato or DsRed responded to FGF2-mediated trans-activation following transfection into RCS cells.
source: These reporters responded well to FGF2-mediated trans-activation following transfection into RCS cells, shown by immunoblot analyses of dTomato and DsRed expression, and live cell imaging (Figure 1F,G; Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot and live cell imaging data in Figures 1F-G and Figure 1—figure supplement 8 demonstrating fluorescent reporter induction.

claim: Expression of the constitutively active FGFR3 mutant K650M in RCS cells induced dTomato or DsRed expression.
source: Expression of the constitutively active FGFR3 mutant K650M (Naski et al., 1996) in RCS cells induced dTomato or DsRed expression, and this expression was reversed by treatment with AZD1480, a chemical inhibitor of FGFR3 (Scuto et al., 2011) (Figure 1H,I; Figure 1—figure supplement 8C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figures 1H-I and Figure 1—figure supplement 8C showing reporter induction by FGFR3 K650M, with citations to characterization studies (Naski et al., 1996; Scuto et al., 2011).

claim: AZD1480 treatment reversed dTomato or DsRed expression induced by FGFR3 K650M in RCS cells.
source: Expression of the constitutively active FGFR3 mutant K650M (Naski et al., 1996) in RCS cells induced dTomato or DsRed expression, and this expression was reversed by treatment with AZD1480, a chemical inhibitor of FGFR3 (Scuto et al., 2011) (Figure 1H,I; Figure 1—figure supplement 8C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figures 1H-I and Figure 1—figure supplement 8C showing inhibition of reporter expression by AZD1480.

claim: A total of 37 full-length human wild-type RTKs were cloned and expressed in 293T cells.
source: A total of 37 full-length human wild-type (wt) RTKs were cloned into the pcDNA3.1 vector in frame with a C-terminal V5/6xHis epitope, expressed in 293T cells, and verified by immunoblot (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figures 2 and 3 showing expression of 37 wild-type RTKs.

claim: A total of 254 wild-type and mutant RTK variants were prepared and analyzed for EGR1 induction.
source: A total of 254 wt and mutant RTK variants were prepared this way, expressed in 293T cells, and analyzed for EGR1 induction.
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation and analysis of 254 RTK variants, with results shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: 30 wild-type RTKs (81%) induced EGR1 when expressed in 293T cells.
source: The results showed that 30 wt RTKs (81%) and 154 (71%) of their mutants induced EGR1 when expressed in 293T cells (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 4 showing EGR1 induction by 30 out of 37 wild-type RTKs.

claim: 154 RTK mutants (71%) induced EGR1 when expressed in 293T cells.
source: The results showed that 30 wt RTKs (81%) and 154 (71%) of their mutants induced EGR1 when expressed in 293T cells (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 4 showing EGR1 induction by 154 out of 217 RTK mutants tested.

claim: Three wild-type RTKs (FGFR3, TIE, VEGFR1) induced EGR1 expression but were not found to be phosphorylated.
source: Three wt RTKs (FGFR3, TIE, VEGFR1) and 27 mutants induced EGR1 expression but were not found to be phosphorylated (Figures 2–4).
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figures 2-4 showing EGR1 induction without detectable phosphorylation for these RTKs.

claim: All five active FGFR3 mutants associated with skeletal dysplasia and cancer induced EGR1.
source: The most notable example is FGFR3, as all five active mutants associated with skeletal dysplasia and cancer (Kant et al., 2015; Passos-Bueno et al., 1999; Carter et al., 2015) induced EGR1, but only K650M FGFR3 was found to be phosphorylated by an antibody recognizing FGFR phosphorylation at Y653/Y654.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing EGR1 induction by FGFR3 mutants, with citations to disease associations (Kant et al., 2015; Passos-Bueno et al., 1999; Carter et al., 2015).

claim: Pseudokinases lacking catalytic activity (ROR1, ROR2, RYK, ERBB3) did not induce EGR1.
source: The pseudokinases lacking catalytic activity (ROR1, ROR2, RYK, ERBB3) were among the RTKs that did not induce EGR1, along with RTKs that did not autophosphorylate after expression in 293T cells (TYRO3, INSRR, ROS1) (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figures 2 and 3 showing lack of EGR1 induction by pseudokinases, consistent with their known lack of catalytic activity.

claim: RTKs that did not autophosphorylate after expression in 293T cells (TYRO3, INSRR, ROS1) did not induce EGR1.
source: The pseudokinases lacking catalytic activity (ROR1, ROR2, RYK, ERBB3) were among the RTKs that did not induce EGR1, along with RTKs that did not autophosphorylate after expression in 293T cells (TYRO3, INSRR, ROS1) (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figures 2 and 3 showing lack of both autophosphorylation and EGR1 induction for these RTKs.

claim: 36 mutants failed to induce EGR1 despite being derived from RTKs that induce EGR1 expression.
source: Furthermore, 36 mutants failed to induce EGR1 despite being derived from RTKs that induce EGR1 expression.
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figures 2-4 showing that 36 mutants did not induce EGR1.

claim: 83% of the 36 mutants that failed to induce EGR1 were kinase-inactive mutants.
source: The majority of these mutants (83%) were kinase-inactive mutants (Figures 2–4).
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figures 2-4 showing that most non-inducing mutants were kinase-dead variants.

claim: RTK activation correlated with EGR1 induction in 96% (154 out of 160) of the tested wild-type and mutant RTKs.
source: Overall, the RTK activation correlated with EGR1 induction in 96% (154 out of 160) of the tested wt and mutant RTKs.
evidence: The manuscript presents a quantitative analysis of the correlation between RTK activation (phosphorylation) and EGR1 induction based on data in Figures 2-4.

claim: All of the protein kinase oncogenes recognized to date (apart from JAK and MAPKK kinases not evaluated) are capable of inducing EGR1 expression in 293T cells.
source: Taken together, we have demonstrated that, apart from the JAK and MAPKK kinases not evaluated in this study, all of the protein kinase oncogenes recognized to date (Vogelstein et al., 2013) are capable of inducing EGR1 expression in 293T cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figures 2-4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing EGR1 induction by protein kinase oncogenes, with reference to the catalog of oncogenes (Vogelstein et al., 2013).

claim: Chronic myeloid leukemia is a clonal myeloproliferative disorder characterized by a t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation that produces a cytoplasmic BCR-ABL fusion protein with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity.
source: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a clonal myeloproliferative disorder characterized by a t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation that produces a cytoplasmic BCR-ABL fusion protein with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity (Zhao et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Zhao et al., 2002) describing the molecular basis of CML.

claim: The suppression of BCR-ABL catalytic activity with tyrosine kinase inhibitors has greatly improved CML prognosis, effectively turning a once fatal cancer into a manageable chronic disease.
source: The suppression of BCR-ABL catalytic activity with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) has greatly improved CML prognosis, effectively turning a once fatal cancer into a manageable chronic disease.
evidence: The claim reflects established clinical knowledge about the impact of TKI therapy on CML outcomes.

claim: Several generations of BCR-ABL TKIs have been developed to improve efficacy and overcome BCR-ABL resistance to first generation TKIs caused by mutations and gene amplifications.
source: Several generations of BCR-ABL TKIs have been developed to improve efficacy and overcome the BCR-ABL resistance to first generation TKIs caused by mutations and gene amplifications (Hochhaus et al., 2008; Cortes et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hochhaus et al., 2008; Cortes et al., 2013) describing TKI development.

claim: Some TKIs, such as ponatinib, can cause severe toxicity in CML patients and even lead to discontinuation of the therapy.
source: However, some TKIs, such as ponatinib, can cause severe toxicity in CML patients and even lead to discontinuation of the therapy (Modugno, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Modugno, 2014) describing ponatinib toxicity.

claim: All tested BCR-ABL TKIs inhibited RTKs that had already been reported as targets in literature, with exception of LTK and INSR.
source: Figure 5A shows that all tested TKIs inhibited RTKs that had already been reported as targets in literature (Supplementary file 1E), with exception of LTK and INSR, which were identified as two novel targets for nilotinib (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 5A and compares findings to previously reported targets in Supplementary file 1E.

claim: Osimertinib is a mutant-selective EGFR inhibitor, with 200-fold selectivity for EGFR mutants T790M and L858R over the wild-type EGFR.
source: Osimertinib is a mutant-selective EGFR inhibitor, with 200-fold selectivity for EGFR mutants T790M and L858R over the wt EGFR (Cross et al., 2014; Finlay et al., 2014; Jiang and Zhou, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cross et al., 2014; Finlay et al., 2014; Jiang and Zhou, 2014) characterizing osimertinib selectivity.

claim: Osimertinib binds to the outer edge of the EGFR ATP binding pocket through a covalent bond with Cys797.
source: Crystallographic studies indicate that osimertinib binds to the outer edge of the EGFR ATP binding pocket through a covalent bond with Cys797 (Yosaatmadja et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to crystallographic studies (Yosaatmadja et al., 2015).

claim: Osimertinib was approved for clinical use in lung carcinoma in 2015.
source: Osimertinib (AZD9291) is recently described inhibitor of EGFR catalytic activity, and was approved for clinical use in lung carcinoma in 2015 (Cross et al., 2014; Greig and Approval, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cross et al., 2014; Greig and Approval, 2016) describing osimertinib approval.

claim: Osimertinib showed inhibitory activity against EGFR, ERBB2 and ERBB4, but not for the other 26 RTKs and 99 mutants tested.
source: We observed inhibitory activity for osimertinib against EGFR, ERBB2 and ERBB4, but not for the other 26 RTKs and 99 mutants (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 5B showing osimertinib activity profile across 30 RTKs and 116 mutants.

claim: LTK mutants D535N and L844I associate with multiple myeloma and stomach carcinoma, respectively.
source: These included the D535N and L844I mutants, which associate with multiple myeloma and stomach carcinoma (Hucthagowder et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2009), respectively, and the W831C and H608Y substitutions found in the Cosmic and VarSome databases.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hucthagowder et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2009) describing disease associations of LTK mutants.

claim: Osimertinib activity against LTK was confirmed by suppression of the autophosphorylation of LTK expressed in 293T cells.
source: The osimertinib activity was confirmed by suppression of the autophosphorylation of LTK expressed in 293T cells, and by inhibition of LTK-mediated phosphorylation of recombinant STAT1 substrate in cell-free kinase assays (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 5C showing osimertinib-mediated suppression of LTK autophosphorylation.

claim: Osimertinib inhibited LTK-mediated phosphorylation of recombinant STAT1 substrate in cell-free kinase assays.
source: The osimertinib activity was confirmed by suppression of the autophosphorylation of LTK expressed in 293T cells, and by inhibition of LTK-mediated phosphorylation of recombinant STAT1 substrate in cell-free kinase assays (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents kinase assay data in Figure 5D showing osimertinib-mediated inhibition of LTK activity in cell-free assays.

claim: In-cell profiling enables the evaluation of receptor tyrosine activity in a complex environment of regulatory networks that affect signal initiation, propagation and feedback.
source: In-cell profiling enables the evaluation of receptor tyrosine activity in a complex environment of regulatory networks that affect signal initiation, propagation and feedback.
evidence: The claim is a conceptual statement about the advantages of in-cell profiling, supported by the overall experimental approach of the study.

claim: RTKs form multiprotein complexes at the cell membrane that mediate signal initiation and propagation, as well as feedback control mechanisms.
source: Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) form multiprotein complexes at the cell membrane that mediate signal initiation and propagation, as well as feedback control mechanisms (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010) describing RTK signaling complexes.

claim: Cell-free activity profiling may only uncover chemicals that directly target RTK catalytic function.
source: While cell-free activity profiling may only uncover chemicals that directly target RTK catalytic function, in-cell profiling confers several additional benefits that could improve the drug development process.
evidence: The claim is a conceptual statement about the limitations of cell-free profiling compared to in-cell profiling.

claim: In-cell profiling may identify biological pathways that naturally oppose the signaling of a certain RTK, and can then be therapeutically exploited.
source: In-cell profiling may identify biological pathways that naturally oppose the signaling of a certain RTK, and can then be therapeutically exploited (Wendt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Wendt et al., 2015) and represents a conceptual advantage of in-cell profiling.

claim: In-cell activity profiling is applicable to disease-specific in vitro and in vivo models.
source: Furthermore, this approach may also enable the targeting of RTKs in non-signaling states, via interference either with their expression, maturation and transport to the cell membrane or their internalization and degradation. Finally, in-cell activity profiling is applicable to disease-specific in vitro and in vivo models.
evidence: The claim is a conceptual statement about the applicability of in-cell profiling to disease models.

claim: Chronic diseases caused by pathological RTK signaling, such as diabetes, pulmonary hypertension, chronic kidney disease, or developmental disorders, are poorly represented in current clinic.
source: This is important in the development of therapeutics for chronic diseases caused by pathological RTK signaling, such as diabetes, pulmonary hypertension, chronic kidney disease, or developmental disorders (Fountas et al., 2015; ten Freyhaus et al., 2012; Harskamp et al., 2016; Laederich and Horton, 2012), all of which are poorly represented in current clinic (Bamborough, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Fountas et al., 2015; ten Freyhaus et al., 2012; Harskamp et al., 2016; Laederich and Horton, 2012; Bamborough, 2012).

claim: Several important oncogenes and downstream targets of RTK signaling, such as RAS, appear not druggable directly.
source: Lastly, several important oncogenes and downstream targets of RTK signaling, such as RAS, appear not druggable directly (Cox et al., 2014) and thus the inhibitors of their signaling may only be discovered via in-cell activity profiling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Cox et al., 2014) discussing the challenges of directly targeting RAS.

claim: Existing toolkits for in-cell RTK activity profiling provide only partial solutions for the development of RTK inhibitors.
source: However, the existing toolkits for in-cell RTK activity profiling provide only partial solutions for the development of RTK inhibitors, as they only focus on a few RTKs or their disease-associated mutants (Supplementary file 1A), are technically or instrumentally challenging, or require the development of RTK-specific tools (Ni et al., 2006; Inglés-Prieto et al., 2015; Regot et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ni et al., 2006; Inglés-Prieto et al., 2015; Regot et al., 2014) and comparison in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The strong effect of ERK on gene transcription could be exploited in the development of reporters that are applicable to the activity profiling of many different RTKs.
source: Hence, the strong effect of ERK on gene transcription could be exploited in the development of reporters that are applicable to the activity profiling of many different RTKs (Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Yang et al., 2003) and represents the conceptual basis for the reporter development.

claim: The fluorescent pKrox24 reporters could improve the interpretation of HTS screening data by readily eliminating false-positive hits based on cell toxicity.
source: Cells can be viewed any time during the screening, and this characteristic of HTS would enable researchers to detect false-positive hits based on the inhibition of dTomato and DsRed expression by cell-toxic compounds through mechanisms unrelated to the target protein kinase. Hence, these reporters could improve the interpretation of HTS screening data by readily eliminating false-positive hits.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the advantages of fluorescent reporters in high-throughput screening.

claim: RTKs are targeted in their natural conformation, with post-translational modifications and in the cell metabolic environment during in-cell profiling.
source: First, RTKs are targeted in their natural conformation, with post-translational modifications and in the cell metabolic environment.
evidence: The claim is a conceptual statement about the advantages of in-cell profiling.

claim: The protein-protein interactions involved in signal transduction through the RTK-associated signaling complexes, downstream elements, or effector pathways may be targeted during in-cell profiling, increasing the chance of success.
source: The protein-protein interactions involved in signal transduction through the RTK-associated signaling complexes, downstream elements, or effector pathways may also be targeted, increasing the chance of success.
evidence: The claim is a conceptual statement about the advantages of in-cell profiling.

claim: In-cell profiling may enable the targeting of RTKs in non-signaling states, via interference with their expression, maturation and transport to the cell membrane or their internalization and degradation.
source: Furthermore, this approach may also enable the targeting of RTKs in non-signaling states, via interference either with their expression, maturation and transport to the cell membrane or their internalization and degradation.
evidence: The claim is a conceptual statement about potential applications of in-cell profiling.

claim: Nilotinib inhibits expression of transfected FGFR2, MET and RON at 2 and 5 μM concentrations.
source: Evidence demonstrating that 2 and 5 μM nilotinib inhibits expression of transfected FGFR2, MET and RON.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D showing reduced protein levels of FGFR2, MET and RON upon nilotinib treatment.

claim: Nilotinib inhibits LTK and INSR autophosphorylation.
source: Inhibition of LTK and INSR autophosphorylation by nilotinib.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E showing reduced autophosphorylation of LTK and INSR upon nilotinib treatment.

claim: The pKrox24 reporter system is based on the promoter sequences of the ERK target gene EGR1.
source: Here, we report the engineering of one such system, which is based on the promoter sequences of the ERK target gene EGR1 (Early growth response 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the development of reporters based on EGR1 promoter sequences.

claim: The pKrox24 reporter system is applicable to simple in-cell activity profiling of most protein kinase oncogenes.
source: We demonstrate that the EGR1-based reporter system is applicable to simple in-cell activity profiling of most protein kinase oncogenes.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that the reporter responds to activation of 30 RTKs and 154 mutants, as well as additional non-receptor kinases.
